sentences.text: The skull of the holotype measures roughly 20.5 cm in length.
Its wingspan reached about 1 meter, larger than most early monofenestratans.
Fossils were uncovered in 2007 at the Schaudiberg Quarry near Mühlheim in Bavaria, Germany.
The holotype specimen entered the Lauer Foundation collection in Illinois in January 2024.
The genus name honors René and Bruce Lauer for their work making Solnhofen fossils accessible to science.
The specific epithet ‘vitriolus’ refers to the pitted texture on the holotype that resembles damage from sulphuric acid.
The animal was formally named in 2026 following its discovery.
It co-existed with Makrodactylus, Skiphosoura, and Rhamphodactylus, taxa that are likely close relatives.
Shared features with Skiphosoura include similar tooth shape and spacing, a strongly curved pteroid bone, and robust mandibles and femurs, suggesting comparable feeding habits.
Compared with Skiphosoura, Laueropterus possessed a proportionally longer and shallower snout and a less conspicuous premaxillary crest.
It is placed within the early pterosaur clade Monofenestrata.
Hone assigned it to Monofenestrata based on its large skull bearing a single nasoantorbital fenestra and elongated neck vertebrae.
Short metacarpals and first wing phalanges indicate it falls outside the more derived Pterodactyloidea.
Laueropterus lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically the Tithonian age, in the Mörnsheim Formation of Germany.
